```{r setup}
library(mylm)
```

## 1. Introduction

The `mylm` package provides a basic implementation of ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression, reproducing the main functionality of `stats::lm()`. Regression coefficients are estimated by solving the normal equations:

$$
X^T X \hat{\beta} = X^T y
$$

The package provides `mylm()` for model fitting, `print()` for displaying fitted models, `summary()` for statistical inference, and `predict()` for generating predictions.

## 2. Basic Usage

### Fitting a model

We first fit a multiple linear regression model using the built-in `mtcars` dataset, with fuel efficiency (`mpg`) as the response and vehicle weight (`wt`) and horsepower (`hp`) as predictors.

```{r}
fit = mylm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
fit
```

### Model summary

The `summary()` method reports coefficient estimates, standard errors, t-statistics, p-values, residual summaries, R-squared, adjusted R-squared, and the overall F-statistic.

```{r}
summary(fit)
```

### Prediction

The `predict()` method uses estimated regression coefficients to predict the response for new observations.

```{r}
newdata = data.frame(wt = c(2.5, 3.0), hp = c(100, 150))
predict(fit, newdata = newdata)
```

## 3. Correctness: Comparison with `lm()`

To evaluate the correctness of `mylm()`, we compare its results with those of `stats::lm()` using `all.equal()`.

This function returns `TRUE` when two objects are equal within a specified numerical tolerance. Small numerical differences may occur due to floating-point calculations.

### Example 1: Continuous predictors (`mtcars`)

We compare the results of a multiple linear regression model with two continuous predictors.

```{r}
fit_my = mylm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)
fit_lm = lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars)

s_my = summary(fit_my)
s_lm = summary(fit_lm)

all.equal(unname(fit_my$coefficients), unname(coef(fit_lm)))
all.equal(s_my$coefficients, s_lm$coefficients)
all.equal(s_my$sigma, s_lm$sigma)
all.equal(s_my$r.squared, s_lm$r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$adj.r.squared, s_lm$adj.r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$fstatistic, s_lm$fstatistic)
all.equal(unname(fit_my$fitted.values), unname(fitted(fit_lm)))
all.equal(
  unname(predict(fit_my, newdata)),
  unname(predict(fit_lm, newdata))
)
```

### Example 2: Factor predictor

This example uses the number of cylinders (`cyl`) as a categorical
predictor. The model includes both a continuous predictor (`wt`)
and a factor predictor (`factor(cyl)`).

```{r}
fit_my = mylm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
fit_lm = lm(mpg ~ wt + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)

s_my = summary(fit_my)
s_lm = summary(fit_lm)

all.equal(unname(fit_my$coefficients), unname(coef(fit_lm)))
all.equal(s_my$coefficients, s_lm$coefficients)
all.equal(s_my$sigma, s_lm$sigma)
all.equal(s_my$r.squared, s_lm$r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$adj.r.squared, s_lm$adj.r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$fstatistic, s_lm$fstatistic)
all.equal(unname(fit_my$fitted.values), unname(fitted(fit_lm)))
```

### Example 3: Interaction term

We also evaluate a regression model containing an interaction
between weight and horsepower. The formula `wt * hp` includes
both main effects and their interaction.

```{r}
fit_my = mylm(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)
fit_lm = lm(mpg ~ wt * hp, data = mtcars)

s_my = summary(fit_my)
s_lm = summary(fit_lm)

all.equal(unname(fit_my$coefficients), unname(coef(fit_lm)))
all.equal(s_my$coefficients, s_lm$coefficients)
all.equal(s_my$sigma, s_lm$sigma)
all.equal(s_my$r.squared, s_lm$r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$adj.r.squared, s_lm$adj.r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$fstatistic, s_lm$fstatistic)
all.equal(unname(fit_my$fitted.values), unname(fitted(fit_lm)))
```

### Example 4: Simulated data

We generate a dataset with 500 observations and five independent standard normal predictors. The response is generated from a linear model with known regression coefficients and normally distributed random errors.

The true coefficients are 1 for the intercept and (2, -1, 0.5, 0, 3) for the five predictors.

```{r}
set.seed(625)
n = 500
p = 5

X = matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
colnames(X) = paste0("x", 1:p)

beta_true = c(1, 2, -1, 0.5, 0, 3)
y = drop(cbind(1, X) %*% beta_true) + rnorm(n)

sim_data = data.frame(y = y, X)

fit_my = mylm(y ~ ., data = sim_data)
fit_lm = lm(y ~ ., data = sim_data)

s_my = summary(fit_my)
s_lm = summary(fit_lm)

all.equal(unname(fit_my$coefficients), unname(coef(fit_lm)))
all.equal(s_my$coefficients, s_lm$coefficients)
all.equal(s_my$sigma, s_lm$sigma)
all.equal(s_my$r.squared, s_lm$r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$adj.r.squared, s_lm$adj.r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$fstatistic, s_lm$fstatistic)
all.equal(unname(fit_my$fitted.values), unname(fitted(fit_lm)))
```
### Example 5: Model without an intercept

For models without an intercept (e.g. `y ~ x - 1`), `lm()` computes
R-squared using the uncentered total sum of squares, and the F-statistic has `p` instead of `p - 1` numerator degrees of freedom. `mylm()` follows the same conventions.

```{r}
fit_my = mylm(mpg ~ wt + hp - 1, data = mtcars)
fit_lm = lm(mpg ~ wt + hp - 1, data = mtcars)

s_my = summary(fit_my)
s_lm = summary(fit_lm)

all.equal(unname(fit_my$coefficients), unname(coef(fit_lm)))
all.equal(s_my$coefficients, s_lm$coefficients)
all.equal(s_my$sigma, s_lm$sigma)
all.equal(s_my$r.squared, s_lm$r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$adj.r.squared, s_lm$adj.r.squared)
all.equal(s_my$fstatistic, s_lm$fstatistic)
all.equal(unname(fit_my$fitted.values), unname(fitted(fit_lm)))
```

These examples examine whether `mylm()` produces results consistent with `lm()` across different model specifications and sample sizes.

## 4. Efficiency: `bench::mark()`

We use `bench::mark()` to compare the computational efficiency of `mylm()` and `stats::lm()`.

The benchmark measures execution time and memory allocation. We set `check = FALSE` because the two functions return objects with different classes and structures.

### Small data (`mtcars`)

```{r}
bench_small = bench::mark(
  mylm = mylm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars),
  lm   = lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = mtcars),
  check = FALSE
)

bench_small
```

### Larger simulated data

We also perform a benchmark using 10,000 observations and 20 predictors to examine computational performance on a larger dataset.

```{r}
set.seed(625)
n = 10000
p = 20

X = matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)
colnames(X) = paste0("x", 1:p)

y = drop(X %*% rnorm(p)) + rnorm(n)
big_data = data.frame(y = y, X)

bench_large = bench::mark(
  mylm = mylm(y ~ ., data = big_data),
  lm   = lm(y ~ ., data = big_data),
  check = FALSE
)

bench_large
```

### Benchmark interpretation

On both datasets, `mylm()` and `lm()` have very similar median execution times. On the larger simulated dataset, `mylm()` is slightly faster. This is expected: for a moderate number of predictors, solving the normal equations requires fewer operations than a QR decomposition, and much of the running time of both functions is spent on processing the formula and building the design matrix with `model.frame()` and `model.matrix()`.

`mylm()` allocates somewhat more memory than `lm()`, because it forms the transpose of the design matrix explicitly and computes standard errors, t-statistics, and p-values at fitting time, whereas `lm()` defers these calculations to `summary()`.

## 5. Summary

The `mylm` package provides an implementation of ordinary least squares regression using the normal equations. It supports multiple predictors, categorical variables, interaction terms, statistical summaries, and prediction.

Correctness is evaluated through comparisons with `stats::lm()` on real and simulated datasets, while computational efficiency is evaluated using `bench::mark()`.

Although the normal-equation approach is straightforward to implement and understand, it may be less numerically stable than the QR decomposition used by `lm()`, particularly for ill-conditioned design matrices.
